segments.title: The Continental System and Britain's Baltic lifeline
segments.body: The 1807 expedition grew from a struggle over commerce and access to northern Europe. Napoleon's Continental System aimed to exclude Britain from European markets, while Britain relied on Baltic naval stores and trade through the North Sea. Denmark's apparent movement into the French system threatened those supplies and routes. Copenhagen therefore became part of Britain's effort to protect its economy and maritime access.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts 1801 and 1807 and identifies the Continental System, Baltic stores, and North Sea trade as Britain's concern.

segments.summary: The 1807 expedition grew from Napoleon's Continental System and Britain's dependence on Baltic supplies and North Sea trade.

segments.title: Parker's signal and Nelson's blind eye
segments.body: Admiral Hyde Parker held overall command in 1801 because Nelson's conduct around Lady Hamilton had weakened confidence in him. Parker's signal may have been intended to give Nelson discretion to withdraw if the battle turned against him. Nelson put a telescope to his blind eye and continued the attack, creating the battle's best-known anecdote. British ships then forced the harbour and captured Danish vessels, setting a precedent that made Denmark's renewed exposure in 1807 more striking.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Parker's command, the signal that may have allowed withdrawal, Nelson's blind-eye response, and the capture of Danish ships.

segments.summary: The blind-eye episode explains how Nelson could continue the 1801 attack after Admiral Hyde Parker signalled from the supporting force.

segments.title: An unready Danish fleet concentrated at Copenhagen
segments.body: Six years after the first attack, Anglo-Danish communications again broke down while Denmark moved toward French alignment. Copenhagen had roughly 5,000 regular troops and a similar militia force available for defence. The Danish fleet was gathered in the capital, unready for sea, and smaller than the expedition Britain could bring against it. Concentration turned the fleet into a fixed target and left Denmark with little room to contest British control of the approaches.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the diplomatic breakdown, the limited Copenhagen garrison, and a concentrated Danish fleet that was neither ready for sea nor equal to the coming British force.

segments.summary: Denmark repeated its central vulnerability from 1801 by leaving an unready fleet concentrated in a lightly defended capital.

segments.title: The Dardanelles comparison: adapt after an attack
segments.body: Earlier attempts to force the Dardanelles show a cycle of attack and defensive adaptation. Ottoman preparations made a return passage difficult, although a later British attempt still succeeded. By World War I, another attack was beaten off and the defenders strengthened the straits against a repeat. Copenhagen provides the contrast: six years after 1801, Britain could return for a similar purpose and again find the Danish fleet exposed in the capital.

evidence.note: The transcript uses repeated attempts at the Dardanelles to argue that defenders normally learn from an attack and deny the same tactics another easy success.

segments.summary: The Dardanelles comparison focuses on how defenders learn between attacks, making Denmark's repeated exposure at Copenhagen the exception.

segments.title: Denmark's strategic bind and its naval consequences
segments.body: Denmark faced a credible threat whichever alignment it chose. Refusing Napoleon while sharing a land frontier with his sphere risked invasion, so accommodation with France could appear safer. French alignment also made British naval intervention predictable because Denmark controlled a fleet and sat near routes Britain considered vital. A seafaring state expecting that response needed to defend its navy or give it room to operate at sea; Denmark did neither.

evidence.note: The transcript weighs the danger of refusing Napoleon against the predictable Royal Navy response and argues that Denmark needed either to defend its navy or put it to sea.

segments.summary: Denmark faced a real choice between French invasion by land and British attack by sea, but French alignment demanded naval preparations Copenhagen had not made.

segments.title: What it meant to "Copenhagen" an enemy
segments.body: In this usage, to "Copenhagen" an opponent meant taking it by surprise and seizing everything needed for resistance. The British also landed troops in 1807, unlike the predominantly naval attack of 1801. The second expedition joined sea power with troops ashore. That sudden, comprehensive seizure made Copenhagen a verb.

evidence.note: The transcript defines the term and contrasts the 1807 use of ground forces with the first battle.

segments.summary: In this shorthand, to "Copenhagen" an opponent meant taking it by surprise and seizing the means of resistance.

segments.title: Narrow waters, shore guns, and mortar ships
segments.body: Copenhagen's narrow channels should have exposed an attacking fleet to concentrated fire from prepared shore positions. Land batteries could mount guns free from many shipboard constraints and use heated shot against wooden hulls. British mortar vessels countered that advantage with specialist weapons supervised by Royal Artillery officers alongside naval gunners. With a deep pool of mathematical and gunnery expertise focused on only one or two mortars, these ships could deliver unusually accurate bombardment. Their fire pushed back the defences and helped Nelson's force close with and capture Danish ships.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses defended channels, heated shot, mortar vessels, artillery specialists, and the approach that enabled Nelson's manoeuvre.

segments.summary: The 1801 battle shows how narrow channels and shore batteries favoured a prepared defender, while specialist British mortar ships helped open the way for Nelson.

segments.title: Gambier's experience and the Basque Roads dispute
segments.body: James Gambier was an experienced admiral with a long career. The episode also notes his support for education and that Gambier, Ohio, was named in part for him. His best-known controversy followed the Battle of the Basque Roads, where Thomas Cochrane and another admiral accused him of cowardice for refusing to pursue French ships onto dangerous rocks. The pursuit promised prize money but exposed British ships and crews to losses while the French were already wrecking themselves. Political rivalry and financial interests hung over the accusations. The dispute concerns a command judgment: whether further risk could produce enough military gain.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces Gambier and Cathcart, then covers Gambier's experience, educational legacy, and Basque Roads controversy.

segments.summary: James Gambier's long service, support for education, and cautious decision at the Battle of the Basque Roads frame the later accusations against him.

segments.title: Cathcart's overlooked role in coalition diplomacy
segments.body: William Cathcart is easy to overlook beside better-known commanders of the Napoleonic Wars. His career included command in Scotland and an expedition to Hanover, followed by service in Russia as ambassador and military commissioner. That work helped coordinate the alliance opposing Napoleon during the wars of liberation. His diplomatic and military experience helps explain why he could direct a large expedition containing other senior generals.

evidence.note: The transcript reviews Cathcart's commands in Scotland and Hanover and his later work in Russia coordinating the alliance against Napoleon.

segments.summary: William Cathcart's later service in Russia shows why the army commander brought diplomatic as well as military experience to Copenhagen.

segments.title: Cathcart's army and the weight of the expedition
segments.body: Several lieutenant generals and major generals served under Cathcart, supporting his authority as the expedition's acting general despite uncertainty over his formal rank. Arthur Wellesley led the reserve, which would do much of the fighting, while the King's German Legion formed a four-brigade division. Guards and line brigades added depth to the army. Engineers, 84 field guns, and 101 siege guns supplied the tools for a formal attack on the city. This was a major land force capable of applying pressure alongside the fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript reviews Cathcart's senior subordinates, the expedition's divisions, the King's German Legion, artillery, engineers, and the stated field and siege guns.

segments.summary: Cathcart directed senior generals, the King's German Legion, engineers, and 185 field and siege guns, giving the expedition weight ashore.

segments.title: Why Gambier built the fleet around third rates
segments.body: Prince of Wales, a 98-gun second rate, was the only ship above the third rate in Gambier's initial force. The rest included solid fighting ships such as Captain, Goliath, Hercules, Orion, Resolution, Spencer, and Vanguard. Gambier's seniority gave him enough influence to request a first rate if he wanted one. He chose a workmanlike fleet and left the navy's largest ships available for other commands. Even his vice admiral received a third-rate flagship, showing that operational fit mattered more than prestige.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Prince of Wales, the third-rate-heavy force, several named ships, and Gambier's willingness to leave first rates for other operations.

segments.summary: Gambier chose capable 74-gun and 64-gun third rates for Copenhagen, preserving scarce first rates for operations elsewhere.

segments.title: A second-rate flagship chosen for command visibility
segments.body: Second rates combined much of a first rate's strength and height with a shorter hull, which made them slower and less handy than many first or third rates. Prince of Wales offered 98 guns, but its broadside advantage over a 74 was modest in this context. Its tall masts gave Gambier a better view for directing a large operation. He also accepted commodores instead of adding rear admirals at the outset. A two-captain arrangement divided ship handling from flag administration and gave the command team more capacity to organize the fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript compares second rates with other rates, explains Gambier's preference for mast height, and describes the two-captain arrangement.

segments.summary: Gambier selected the 98-gun Prince of Wales for its mast height and the view it gave him across a complex combined operation.

segments.title: Reinforcements under experienced captains
segments.body: The fleet's captain list includes officers with substantial service, reinforcing the quality of a force built largely from third rates. The Admiralty later sent another rear admiral with Minotaur, Superb, Valiant, Inflexible, Defence, Mars, Agamemnon, and African. These were capable ships under seasoned officers, even though the expedition lacked a concentration of first rates. Their arrival shows the operation's strategic priority and gave Gambier more depth for a campaign involving both sea and land forces.

evidence.note: The transcript names captains in the initial force and lists the additional rear admiral and ships sent to reinforce Gambier.

segments.summary: A roster of experienced captains and another rear admiral shows how much command talent the Admiralty committed to Copenhagen.

segments.title: Third rates for Copenhagen's shallow approaches
segments.body: Gambier's fleet composition matched the water and the mission. Third rates could fight any likely opponent while reaching farther into shallow approaches than the navy's largest ships. A 74-gun ship still delivered formidable combat power, so choosing it did not mean accepting a weak battle line. The second-rate Prince of Wales served a different purpose: its high masts improved the commander's view across the operation. Together, the choices balanced fighting strength, access, and command visibility.

evidence.note: The transcript explains why Gambier preferred third rates for combat and shallow-water work and Prince of Wales for command visibility.

segments.summary: Third rates offered the strength to face likely opponents and enough handiness to work toward Copenhagen's shallow approaches.

segments.title: Naval diplomacy before the attack
segments.body: Cathcart arrived on 12 August, and the assembled fleet remained in view before major action began in September. That pause made the expedition a display of military power as well as a force ready to fight. British leaders expected the memory of 1801 to encourage Denmark to negotiate before another attack. The pressure failed, and the same vulnerability that the demonstration exposed became the basis of the coming operation.

evidence.note: The transcript dates Cathcart's arrival, describes the force waiting through August, and calls the display an attempt at naval diplomacy.

segments.summary: The British force waited visibly through August, using the threat of another Copenhagen attack to press Denmark toward negotiation.
